newsitem.title: IRAQ: Kurd family torn between U.S. and Saddam's shadow.
newsitem.headline: Kurd family torn between U.S. and Saddam's shadow.

text.p: For most of the hundreds of Kurds who worked as U.S. employees in northern Iraq, being evacuated to safety in the United States is a dream come true.
But for members of at least one family who could leave, the pull of their home in Iraqi Kurdistan remained greater than the lure of the United States or the fear of Saddam Hussein.
"We fled Saddam and went to the mountains in 1974 and again in 1991 and both times our house was looted and we had to start over with our lives," explained Layik, 44, the family matriarch.
"I'm too old to do this. If we went to America and decided to come back there would be nothing left of my house. My husband and my children can go, but I'm staying."
Her husband, 58-year-old Hussam, smiles with exasperated indulgence. He is the boss in the family but the moral centre of gravity rests with his wife.
Leaving without her would be unthinkable.

"Our friends and our family are here. What would we do in America?" Hussam said. Fluent in English, Arabic and Kurdish, Hussam is a local headmaster who has worked with journalists and foreign visitors, including U.S. military and civilian personnel, on behalf of one of the Kurdish factions.
"I am begging Hussam to go with us to America," said Moyyad Yunis Rassool, one of hundreds of pro-U.S. Kurds evacuated across the Turkish border on Sunday.
"I warned him Saddam will not forgive or forget a man who welcomed foreign journalists, European parliamentarians and American officals to Kurdistan. He will want his revenge."
Iraq's president has boosted his influence in the region by backing one victorious Kurdish militia against its rival.
Moyyad's son Ahmed, 8, has already secured a promise from his father to visit Disneyland and to buy him a pair of "shoes with wheels" (rollerskates) as soon as they get to America.
Television has familiarised Hussam's children, two boys and two girls ranging in age from 11 to 24, with American popular culture.
They seem eager to go and Hussam is vulnerable to pleas from Moyyad and reporters to consider his children's future.
"No matter what is decided, someone is left unhappy," Hussam explained simply.
Hussam and Layik huddle in their small garden late into the night, quietly weighing the options, exchanging harsh words and shedding tears.
As of now it seemed none of them would leave.
